Chapter 3: The Power of Feedback and Self-Awareness in Breaking Old Patterns
So, you've figured out which habits might be holding you back. Now comes the real challenge—breaking free from them. And let’s be honest, that’s no easy feat. Habits get wired into our routines, making them stubborn and tough to change.
What does it really take? Well, it all starts with self-awareness and a genuine openness to feedback from the people around you.
Think of feedback like a mirror. It shows you things you might not see otherwise—the real impact of what you say and do.
But here’s the tricky part: the higher up you are in an organization, the harder it is to get honest feedback. People might hold back, either because they’re worried about consequences or they just want to avoid awkwardness. That means those blind spots stick around, and unhelpful habits go unchallenged.
So, how do you break through that barrier? It comes down to creating open, trusted channels for feedback. And it’s more than asking, “Hey, what do you think?”
You’ve got to show that you’re really listening—and that you’ll actually do something with what you hear. When your colleagues see that their input matters, they’ll be much more likely to share what they notice.
Imagine a lighthouse for a moment. Feedback is like that guiding beacon, shining light on hidden hazards you’d otherwise miss. Even the most talented navigator can run aground without it. In your own career, feedback helps you avoid those subtle missteps that might undermine your effectiveness.
Now, what are some practical ways to make feedback a part of your routine? Here are a few ideas:
Start by inviting feedback from a wide range of colleagues—not just your closest friends.
Ask open-ended, specific questions about how your behavior affects others.
When someone gives you input, listen. Don’t interrupt or jump in to defend yourself.
Make sure to thank them, no matter what they share.
And after you’ve heard them out, take some time to reflect. Look for patterns or recurring themes.
Here’s something you might find especially helpful: instead of focusing on what went wrong before, try shifting to “feedforward.” That means asking your colleagues for suggestions about what you could do differently next time.
For example, instead of saying, “What did I do wrong in that meeting?” you could ask, “What’s one thing I could try in future meetings to be more effective?” This simple change moves the conversation away from blame and toward collaboration. Suddenly, input feels like a shared effort, not criticism.
At the heart of all this is self-awareness. It’s the foundation for any real change.
Self-awareness means understanding not just your strengths and weaknesses, but also how others see you. And that takes humility—being willing to accept that your self-image might not always match reality.
One of the biggest barriers to self-awareness? Rationalizing or justifying your actions. It’s easy to explain away your own shortcomings, especially if you’re used to achieving a lot. But real growth comes from listening, reflecting, and owning up to your impact.
Building self-awareness isn’t a one-and-done thing. It’s an ongoing journey. Regular check-ins with colleagues, mentors, or coaches can help you stay focused and hold yourself accountable. Over time, even small shifts in your behavior can make a big difference in your relationships—and your effectiveness.
So, here’s the key takeaway: Embracing feedback and cultivating self-awareness are crucial steps in breaking those old, limiting patterns. By seeking out honest input, listening with an open mind, and reflecting on your actions, you’ll set yourself up for real growth and greater impact.
